⚡ A Gauntlet of Challenges — mishna after mishna answered with 'that's only rabbinic law'

overview.title: 📖 Overview: Combining Amounts, and How Far Torah-Law Me'ilah Reaches
overview.subtitle: Meilah 15a–15b
overview.hebrewSource: מְחַוַּורְתָּא, אֵין חַיָּיבִין מִשּׁוּם מְעִילָה אֶלָּא עַל קׇדְשֵׁי בֶּדֶק הַבַּיִת וְעוֹלָה בִּלְבַד
overview.label: The scene:
overview.text: A new mishna opens by establishing which consecrated items 'join together' (מצטרפין) to reach the minimum measures for liability — one peruta for me'ilah, an olive-bulk for piggul/notar/tamei. Rabbi Yannai then makes a striking claim: Torah-level me'ilah applies only to items consecrated for Temple maintenance and to the burnt offering, since only these are 'uniquely for the Lord' — other altar offerings have portions belonging to priests or owners. The Gemara tests this against mishna after mishna that seems to show broader me'ilah, deflecting each with 'that's only by rabbinic law,' before finally locating two separate Torah verses that anchor Torah-level me'ilah for the two categories. The daf then turns to which specific components of an offering combine to reach the required olive-bulk, and closes with items that share a common Torah name.

slides.title: 🔗 What Combines to Reach the Threshold?
slides.subtitle: The new mishna's three categories
rows: Each other, despite having different types of sanctity

callout.label: Why state the first case separately?
callout.text: Even though altar items already combine with maintenance items for me'ilah, the mishna needs a separate first clause because ONLY altar items — never maintenance items — combine for piggul, notar, and tamei liability.

slides.title: ⚡ Rabbi Yannai's Claim, Tested Again and Again
slides.subtitle: Every seemingly contrary mishna gets the same answer

nodes.content: 📜 R' Yannai: Torah-level me'ilah applies only to Temple maintenance and the burnt offering — 'the sacred items OF THE LORD' (Lev. 5:15) means items with NO portion for priests or owners
❓ Challenge 1: our new mishna says ALL altar items combine for me'ilah, not just the burnt offering!
❓ Challenge 2: the opening mishna (2a) says sin/guilt offerings slaughtered in the south ARE subject to me'ilah!
❓ Challenge 3: a dead sin offering incurs me'ilah for any benefit at all (18a)!
✅ Each time: 'That's only by RABBINIC law' — Torah law remains limited to maintenance items and the burnt offering

callout.label: One challenge holds firm:
callout.text: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi's baraita ('all the fat is the Lord's,' Lev. 3:16) is dismissed as a mere 'asmakhta' — textual support, not the actual Torah-law source — keeping the pattern intact.

slides.title: 📜 The Final Resolution: Two Verses, Two Categories
slides.subtitle: Rabbi Yannai's school clarifies what each verse actually teaches
slides.hebrewSource: מֵהַאי קְרָא קׇדְשֵׁי בֶּדֶק הַבַּיִת שָׁמְעִין מִינַּהּ, קׇדְשֵׁי מִזְבֵּחַ לָא שָׁמְעִין מִינַּהּ
slides.label: The correction:
slides.text: A challenge from Ulla (citing Rabbi Yoḥanan, that dead offerings lose me'ilah 'by Torah law') forces a revision: Rabbi Yannai must actually hold that altar-consecrated animals DO carry Torah-level me'ilah while alive — otherwise Ulla's statement makes no sense. The resolution: Leviticus 5:15 ('the sacred items of the Lord') is the source specifically for Temple-maintenance items; altar-consecrated items get their Torah-level me'ilah from a DIFFERENT verse — either 'if a man eat of the sacred items' (Lev. 22:14) or 'all the fat is the Lord's' (Lev. 3:16). Two categories, two independent sources — not one verse stretched to cover everything.

slides.title: 🥩 What Joins Together to Form an Olive-Bulk?
slides.subtitle: New mishna: components of a burnt offering vs. a thanks offering
rows: Meat, fat, fine flour, wine, oil — five items (Rav Huna's mistaken teaching 'in the world' was corrected by Rava to 'in the burnt offering')
The same five, plus the accompanying loaves — six items total
Meat + fat for sprinkling the blood (R' Yehoshua's rule, most offerings)
Must together reach a full olive-bulk — half an olive-bulk of each does NOT suffice, since meat and fat serve different purposes
Meat + fat for a BURNT offering specifically
Even half an olive-bulk of each suffices — since both are equally consumed on the altar, unlike offerings where meat is eaten and fat is burned

callout.label: Chain effect:
callout.text: Whatever combination is enough to permit sprinkling the blood also becomes the threshold for later piggul, notar, and tamei liability — but peace offerings' meat and sacrificial portions never combine for sprinkling, so they never combine for those liabilities either.

slides.title: 🌾 Two More Combining Groups: A Shared Name, and Shared Repugnance
slides.subtitle: Closing mishnayot of the chapter

boxes.title: The Teruma Family
items: Teruma, teruma of the tithe, teruma of demai-tithe, ḥalla, and bikkurim all combine
Reason: ALL are called 'teruma' somewhere in the Torah
Ḥalla: 'you shall set apart teruma' (Num. 15:20); bikkurim: 'the offering of your hand' (Deut. 12:17)

boxes.title: Forbidden Foods
items: All animal carcasses (nevelot) combine with each other
All repugnant creatures (shekatzim) combine with each other
Each category reaches its own olive-bulk (or lentil-bulk, for the eight creeping animals) threshold independently

summary.principle: Combination for the required measure — one peruta for me'ilah, an olive-bulk for piggul/notar/tamei — follows the logic of shared category (altar vs. maintenance, or a shared Torah name), while Torah-level me'ilah itself splits between two independent verses: one for items uniquely 'of the Lord' and one for altar-consecrated animals more broadly.

flowSteps.content: 🔗 New mishna: altar items combine for both me'ilah and piggul/notar/tamei; maintenance items combine only for me'ilah
📜 R' Yannai: Torah-level me'ilah — only maintenance items and the burnt offering (per Lev. 5:15)
⚡ Every challenging mishna deflected as merely rabbinic — until Ulla's statement forces a correction

columns.content: 📜 Two verses: Lev. 5:15 for maintenance items; Lev. 22:14/3:16 for altar-consecrated animals
🥩 Meat+fat combine fully for a burnt offering; only fully for others when each half reaches its own olive-bulk

flowSteps.content: 🎓 Key Principle: combination and Torah-level liability both track precise categorical and textual lines, never a single blanket rule

quiz.q: According to the new mishna, what is unique about items consecrated for the altar compared to items consecrated for Temple maintenance, regarding combination?
o: Altar items never combine with anything
Altar items combine for both me'ilah AND piggul/notar/tamei liability, while maintenance items combine only for me'ilah
Maintenance items combine for piggul but altar items do not
There is no difference between the two
quiz.e: The mishna specifies that only altar-consecrated items combine to reach the olive-bulk threshold for piggul, notar, and tamei liability, since those concepts don't apply to Temple-maintenance items.

quiz.q: According to Rabbi Yannai's original claim, which categories are subject to me'ilah by Torah law?
o: All consecrated items equally
Only items consecrated for Temple maintenance and the burnt offering, since only these are 'uniquely for the Lord'
Only sin and guilt offerings
Nothing is subject to Torah-level me'ilah
quiz.e: Rabbi Yannai derives from Leviticus 5:15 that only items with no portion for priests or owners — Temple maintenance items and the burnt offering — carry Torah-level me'ilah.

quiz.q: How does the Gemara respond to the challenge from Ulla (citing Rabbi Yoḥanan) that dead sacrificial animals lose me'ilah 'by Torah law'?
o: By rejecting Ulla's statement entirely
By revising Rabbi Yannai's position: altar-consecrated animals DO have Torah-level me'ilah, derived from a different verse (Lev. 22:14 or Lev. 3:16) than the one for maintenance items (Lev. 5:15)
By saying Ulla was mistaken about Rabbi Yoḥanan's view
By concluding there is no Torah-level me'ilah anywhere
quiz.e: The Gemara resolves the difficulty by clarifying that Rabbi Yannai's school actually holds there are two separate Torah sources — one for maintenance items and a different one for altar-consecrated animals.

quiz.q: According to Rabbi Yehoshua's rule, when do the meat and fat of a burnt offering combine to permit sprinkling the blood, even if only half an olive-bulk of each remains?
o: Never — a full olive-bulk of each is always required
Always for a burnt offering, since both meat and fat are equally consumed on the altar, unlike other offerings where meat is eaten and fat is burned
Only for peace offerings
Only when the priest is the High Priest
quiz.e: Because a burnt offering is entirely consumed on the altar, its meat and fat serve the identical function, so even half an olive-bulk of each combines to permit sprinkling — unlike other offerings, where they serve different purposes and don't combine that way.

quiz.q: Why do teruma, teruma of the tithe, teruma of demai-tithe, ḥalla, and bikkurim all combine to reach the requisite measure?
o: Because they are all grown in the same season
Because all of them are called 'teruma' somewhere in the Torah
Because they are all consecrated to the altar
Because they share the same olive-bulk measure as meat offerings
quiz.e: The Gemara explains that the shared Torah terminology — each of these items is called 'teruma' in some verse — is what allows them to combine together for the requisite measure.
